items.title: Downtime Manager User Guide
items.text:
Downtime Manager (DTM) records the failures that interrupt or degrade Jefferson Lab's accelerator programs, and reports on them. Operators record downtime as events made of incidents, one per failed system; subject matter experts and Operability review each incident; and the reports turn the records into downtime, repair and availability statistics. DTM also shows the Fast ShutDown (FSD) trips it gets from the FSD system.

At JLab, DTM is at ace.jlab.org/dtm. You can view it without logging in; log in to make changes.

The guide's website has a copy for each release; pick the version the Help tab shows. On GitHub, this guide describes the main branch, which may be newer than the version you are using.

items.title: Contents
items.text:
1. Concepts: events, incidents, restore time, event types, categories, reviews, trips and roles.
  2. Recording downtime: adding, updating and closing events and incidents, hall events, tuning and logbook entries. For operators.
  3. Reviewing incidents: review levels, the SME and OPR reviews, expert emails and Repair Assessment Reports (RARs). For experts and reviewers.
  4. Trips: the FSD trip list.
  5. Reports: the Reports, Operability and Beam Transport tabs, and how they count downtime.
  6. Administration: the Setup tab and settings. For administrators.

items.title: Tabs at a glance
items.text: Tab What it is for Open The events that are open now; start and update downtime here. Events All events, with filters. Trips FSD trips. Reports Downtime, trip and review statistics. Operability The weekly, monthly and annual repair and availability reports, and Joule. RAR Incidents with Repair Assessment Reports, and SAM RARs. Beam Transport Tuning (Beam Transport) incidents. Setup Administrators only: settings, experts and email. Help Version, contacts, documentation and a feedback form.

items.title: Quick start for operators
items.text:
1. When something fails, go to Open. If an event of the right type is already open, select Add Incident on it; otherwise select Add Event.
  2. Give it a title and summary, the time it went down, and the component that failed.
  3. When the system is repaired and handed back, close the incident by setting its Time Up.
  4. When beam is back where it should be, close the event by setting its Time Up.

See Recording downtime for the details.

items.title: Questions and changes
items.text:
Use the feedback form on the Help tab, or contact the content and technical contacts listed there. To suggest a change to this guide, open an issue or pull request on GitHub.

This guide replaces the 2014 "Downtime Manager Guidance" (Rev 1.3) by Randy Michaud, Accelerator Operability; its definitions and guidance that still apply are included here.

items.title: Administration
items.text:
User Guide › Administration

This page is for DTM administrators: users with the dtm-admin role, who see the Setup tab. Being an administrator doesn't make you a reviewer; that is the dtm-reviewer role. See Roles.

items.title: Setup tab
items.text:
Page For Settings The app's settings; see below. Select a row to edit its value. Directory Cache DTM caches users' names, emails and roles, and clears the cache every night at midnight. Clear it, or look up a user or role, after a change in the directory. Users must log out and in again for a role change to apply. Types The event types, read-only. Categories The category and system tree, the alpha categories and each event type's root categories, read-only. Expert List Add or remove a system's subject matter experts (SMEs). Choose the system with Choose.... Email Whether the daily expert emails are on, and Preview or Send Email Now to one SME.

Event types, categories, systems, components and repair groups can't be changed in DTM. At JLab the categories, systems, components and groups come from SRM.

items.title: Alpha categories
items.text: Many reports use the alpha categories as their top level. They must cover all downtime once: none can be inside another, and none can be left out. Including a top-level category would rule out every category under it, and a category that has systems beside it can't be one, since its parent is needed to count those systems. The Beam Transport category must be an alpha category: the NPES schedule allows time for beam transport (tuning), and the Joule report uses it.

items.title: Experts
items.text: When an incident is created or its system changes, the system's experts become the incident's SMEs. Changing the expert list doesn't change incidents that already exist.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Setup › Settings lists the settings with their descriptions. Some changes can break the app or the Settings page itself, so that they can only be undone in the database. Changes made in the database directly take effect after Refresh Cache or a redeploy, and IP_READ_FILTER_ENABLED and IP_READ_URL_PATTERN always need a redeploy.

Setting Effect NOTIFICATION_ENABLED, NOTIFICATION_MESSAGE, NOTIFICATION_LINK_NAME, NOTIFICATION_LINK_URL The banner at the top of every page. HELP_CONTENT_CONTACT, HELP_TECHNICAL_CONTACT The contacts on the Help tab. HELP_DOC_CSV The Help tab's documentation links: URL\|Label items separated by commas (neither can contain a comma). ADMIN_ROLE_NAME The role whose members are listed on the Help tab and get the feedback form's emails. EMAIL_ENABLED Turns on the daily expert emails and the Help tab's feedback emails. EMAIL_TESTING_ENABLED Sends emails to the members of the testlead role instead, for testing. If no member of that role has an email address, expert emails are not sent. EMAIL_EXPERT_CC_LIST Addresses copied on every expert email. EMAIL_SENDER_ADDRESS The sender of feedback emails, and the sender and from address of expert emails. EMAIL_DOMAIN_NAME Added to an expert's username to make the address their emails go to, such as @jlab.org. LOGBOOK_ENABLED, LOGBOOK_LIST Logbook entries for incidents, and the logbooks they go to; see Logbook entries. SRM_DOWNGRADE_ENABLED, SRM_DOWNGRADE_URL The Downgrade Readiness link on incidents of systems that SRM tracks. NPES_SCHEDULE_ENABLED, NPES_SCHEDULE_URL The NPES schedule's budgeted hours on the Joule report. Off, they are 0. IP_READ_FILTER_ENABLED, IP_READ_ALLOWLIST_PATTERN, IP_READ_URL_PATTERN Whether users outside the allowed addresses must log in to view pages. SMOOTHNESS_CDN_ENABLED, SMOOTHNESS_SERVER Where the pages' shared scripts and styles come from.

Server settings, such as where RAR files are stored (RAR_DIR), the logbook server and the bulletin board for escalations, are environment variables; see the README.

items.title: Help tab
items.text: The Help tab shows the version, the contacts, the administrators, the HELP_DOC_CSV links and a feedback form, which emails the administrators. To link this guide from it, add an item such as https://github.com/JeffersonLab/dtm/blob/main/docs/user-guide/README.md|User Guide to HELP_DOC_CSV.

items.title: Concepts
items.text: User Guide › Concepts

items.title: Why record downtime
items.text:
Downtime Manager (DTM) records equipment and system failures that interrupt or degrade the scheduled program, so they can be counted and analyzed. The statistics show which categories, systems and components fail, how often and for how long, and how long the machine takes to recover. Management uses them to decide where to spend maintenance effort and money, so the data is only as useful as it is accurate. Record downtime as it happens: an event that has to be reconstructed later costs time and is less reliable.

DTM is not Beam Time Accounting (BTM). BTM accounts for the hours of beam delivered against the program, for the Department of Energy metrics. DTM records each failure separately, by system, so failures that happen at the same time are each recorded in full, even though beam was only lost once. The two are independent: don't try to make DTM add up to the hours lost in BTM.

items.title: Events and incidents
items.text:
An event is a disruption of a program. Each event has a type, a title, a start (the earliest incident's time down) and an end, its time up, when the program is recovered: beam is back at the expected destination.

An incident is the failure of one system or component inside an event. Every event has at least one incident. A single failure is one event with one incident; when a second system fails while the first is still down, add a second incident to the same event, and so on. Each incident has its own time down (when the component failed) and time up (when it was repaired and handed back to Operations).

Only one event of each type can be open at a time, and events of the same type can't overlap in time. Events of different types are independent and can be open at once: for example a CEBAF Blocked event while Hall C has its own Hall C event.

items.title: Restore time
items.text: The machine usually needs time to recover after the last repair: beam has to be re-established and delivered again. That is the event's restore time: the parts of the event when no incident is open, from the gaps between incidents to the time between the last incident's time up and the event's time up. Closing every incident doesn't close the event; it stays open, and restore time keeps growing, until you set the event's time up.

items.title: Accounting examples
items.text:
These examples, carried over from the original 2014 guidance, show how incidents record each system's downtime separately.

  • One failure. An RF zone fails for 2 hours of an 8-hour shift. Record one event with one RF incident: RF downtime is 2 hours, and BTM records 6 hours of beam.
  • Two failures at once. An RF zone and a magnet box supply both fail for the same 2 hours. Record one event with two incidents, one RF and one magnet, each 2 hours. BTM still records 6 hours of beam.
  • Overlapping failures. An RF zone is down for 2 hours; later a magnet box supply fails for 1 hour and a PSS drop lasts 2 hours, overlapping each other. Each gets its own incident, closed when that system is repaired: RF 2 hours, magnets 1 hour, PSS 2 hours. BTM records 4 hours of beam.

items.title: Event types
items.text:
The event type says which program was affected. An administrator can see the list on Setup › Types; the default ones are:

Type Abbr. Use for CEBAF Blocked BLK Accelerator failures that block the CEBAF program. CEBAF Degraded DGD Accelerator Division repairs that degrade the program but don't block it, such as a failure affecting one hall while CEBAF keeps delivering to others. Degraded events often run for a long time. CEBAF Non-Program NON Failures that don't affect the CEBAF program. CEBAF Tuning TUN Beam transport and tuning time; see Beam transport and tuning. Hall A, B, C, D HLA, HLB, HLC, HLD Problems in an experimental hall that disrupt that hall's physics program. LERF LRF The LERF program.

The distinction between Accelerator Division and Physics Division downtime matters: they are reported separately (it is the difference between BNA and BANU on experimenter time sheets). A hall's own problem belongs in that hall's event, not in a CEBAF event. See Hall events.

Each event type allows only some categories, its root categories, so the component choices in the incident form depend on the type. Setup › Categories lists them under "Type Roots". With the default data:

Type Categories you can choose from CEBAF Blocked CEBAF, Other, Cryo, Facilities CEBAF Degraded, CEBAF Non-Program CEBAF, Other, Cryo, Facilities, Beam Transport CEBAF Tuning Beam Transport Hall A, B, C, D That hall's category, Hall Downtime LERF LERF, Other, Cryo, Facilities, Beam Transport

items.title: Categories, systems and components
items.text:
What failed is recorded as a component. Components belong to systems (equipment with a common function), and systems belong to categories, which form a tree: for example CEBAF › Magnets › Box Supply. Picking a component in the incident form fills in its system and category. At JLab the lists come from SRM, so they match the other accelerator tools; they can't be edited in DTM.

The special component Unknown/Missing is for when the failed component isn't in the list or isn't known. DTM asks you to explain what it was, so the list can be corrected later.

Alpha categories are the categories that reports use as their top level, such as RF, Magnets, Cryo, Beam Transport and Hall A: a flat set, none inside another, chosen to cover the downtime once. They are listed on Setup › Categories.

Repairer groups (workgroups) record who repaired an incident. They have nothing to do with permissions.

items.title: Reviews
items.text:
Every incident is reviewed twice. The reviews are covered in Reviewing incidents.

  • SME review: the system's subject matter experts acknowledge the incident, give a root cause, or upload a Repair Assessment Report (RAR), depending on how long it lasted (its review level: Level Ⅰ under 30 minutes, Level Ⅱ under 4 hours, Level Ⅲ+ 4 hours or more).
  • OPR review: the Operability reviewer checks the incident and records the repairer and solution.

items.title: Trips
items.text: A trip is a short interruption caused by a Fast ShutDown (FSD) system fault. DTM records trips automatically from the FSD system, and they are shown on the Trips tab. A trip that lasts more than 5 minutes should be recorded as a downtime event; most events start as trips. DTM doesn't convert trips into events: you add the event yourself.

items.title: Roles
items.text:
Role Can Anyone, without logging in View the pages and reports. Operator (any logged-in user) Add, edit, close and delete events and incidents, until an incident has been OPR reviewed or its event closed more than 10 hours ago. Edit SME reviews and upload RARs. Reviewer (dtm-reviewer) Everything an Operator can, plus set the OPR reviewer, change reviewed incidents and old events, and edit the Operability review pages. Admin (dtm-admin) The Setup tab and the Activity Audit report. Admin doesn't include Reviewer.

Reviewers choose to act as Reviewer or Operator from the menu next to their name at the top of the page; they start as Reviewer when they log in. Everyone else is shown as Operator. Role changes take effect the next time you log in.

items.title: Recording downtime
items.text:
User Guide › Recording downtime

This page is for operators: how to add, update and close events and incidents. Read Concepts first for what events, incidents and event types are.

items.title: What to record
items.text:
• Record downtime once hot checkout is complete and a beam program is set (beam authorized, beam commissioning, and so on). Failures during a scheduled accelerator maintenance (SAM) period aren't recorded.
  • Record failures that affect the scheduled program, as they happen.
  • Beam studies are part of the scheduled program and are accounted for in BTM, not as downtime.
  • If the program is changed because of a failure, keep the event open until the repair is done and the original program resumes, or until Operability says to close it.
  • An FSD trip that lasts more than 5 minutes should be recorded as an event. See Trips.

items.title: Where to work
items.text:
• Open lists the events that are open now. This is where you start and update downtime during a shift. Its links open the current and previous shift's incident summaries and the wall display.
  • Events lists all events, newest first, 10 to a page, filtered by date range, type, Beam Transport, SME, acknowledgement, event ID or incident ID (open the filter with Choose...).

Click an event's row to expand it. The header shows the type, title, time down and duration (highlighted after 2 hours and again after 4), "(N)" when it has more than one incident, "^" when it is still open, and icons for whether its incidents are SME and OPR reviewed. Expanded, it shows a timeline of its incidents, the restore time and a table of the incidents.

You must be logged in to make changes.

items.title: Adding an event
items.text:
1. On Open (or Events), select Add Event.
  2. On the Observed tab, under Event Information, enter the event Title and choose the Type. Leave Time Up empty for an event that is still going on.
  3. Under Incident Description, the incident Title is the event's title while Same as Event is checked. Enter a Summary of what was observed and, if there is one, the ePAS permit number.
  4. Under Incident Period, Time Down is filled in with the current time; correct it to when the failure happened. Leave Time Up empty while the incident is open.
  5. Under Incident Cause, type at least two letters of the Component and pick it from the list. To browse instead, check Filter by Category/System, choose a category and system, and select ▼ to list the system's components.
  6. Select Save.

Times are entered as DD-MMM-YYYY hh:mm in 24-hour time, such as 02-Nov-2026 14:05; use the date picker or the Now button. Times can't be in the future.

The form checks a few things before it saves:

  • Only one event of each type can be open. If an event of that type is already open, add an incident to it instead.
  • Events of the same type can't overlap in time.
  • If you choose Unknown/Missing as the component, you are asked to explain what component failed.
  • For a hall event you are reminded to set BOOM to BNR mode, if applicable.
  • Choosing Controlled Access or End Station Procedure in a CEBAF Blocked event asks you to confirm, since those belong in hall events.

To record an event that is already over, fill in the event's Time Up and the incident's Time Up. Operators can only add events that ended in the last 10 hours; ask a reviewer for older ones.

items.title: Adding an incident
items.text:
When another system fails during an open event, add an incident to that event rather than starting a new event of the same type.

  1. Expand the event and select Add Incident.
  2. Enter the incident's title, summary, time down and component as for a new event. Append Incident Title adds the incident's title to the event's title ("Original + New"); uncheck it to keep the event's title.
  3. Select Save.

items.title: Updating and closing incidents
items.text:
Select Edit/Close Incident on the incident's row to correct it or close it (once it is closed, the button is Edit Incident; clear its Time Up to reopen it). To close it, set its Time Up to when the system was repaired and handed back to Operations.

The Explained tab holds the review fields. Operators can fill in the Repairer groups and the Solution; only a reviewer can set the OPR Reviewer.

The subject matter experts (SMEs), in Reviewer(s) on the Explained tab, come from the expert list for the incident's system. They are set when the incident is created, and again whenever its system changes; you can change them there too.

items.title: Closing an event
items.text:
When the program is recovered, select Edit/Close Event, set the event's Time Up and select Save. Any incidents still open are closed at the same time. The time up can't be earlier than the last incident's time down or time up.

Once the event is closed the button is Edit Event. To reopen the event, clear its Time Up; you can't while another event of the same type is open. You can also change an event's title and type, as long as it doesn't then overlap another event of the new type.

items.title: Deleting
items.text: Delete Incident deletes an incident; deleting the last one deletes its event too. Delete Event deletes the event with all its incidents. Both ask you to confirm.

items.title: When you can't make changes
items.text:
Operators can't edit, add to or delete:

  • an incident that has been OPR reviewed, or an event that contains one;
  • an event that was closed more than 10 hours ago.

The buttons are hidden in those cases; ask a reviewer.

items.title: Hall events
items.text:
A problem that is unique to an experimental hall and disrupts its program is recorded as that hall's event, not as a CEBAF event. Each hall, CEBAF and LERF have their own events, which are independent of each other and can be open at the same time.

For a hall problem:

  1. Add an event with the hall's type, such as Hall D.
  2. Choose a component from the hall's category or from Hall Downtime, such as Controlled Access, End Station Procedure or Hall Downtime (Unk/Missing).

If the accelerator also fails, while the hall event is open or not, record that in a separate CEBAF event. Don't record problems in several halls as incidents of one CEBAF event: give each hall its own event.

items.title: Beam transport and tuning
items.text:
Program interruptions caused by beam quality rather than a hardware failure, which used to be called "tuning", "tune time" or "unknown", are recorded in the Beam Transport category. Examples are running the locks to fix orbit shifts, cleaning up the orbit after beam loss monitor trips, ion chamber trips due to drift, unexplained beam instabilities, and hall tuning of beam positions.

  • Use the CEBAF Tuning type, which allows only Beam Transport components.
  • Pick the component that is closest to what is happening, such as Orbit, Optics, Injector or Beam Instability.
  • If the instability is caused by a known hardware component, record it as a failure of that component instead.

Tuning is reported separately. The Beam Transport tab reports Beam Transport incidents, and most reports can include them or leave them out. The Joule report's "Tuning, Setup, & Restore" counts CEBAF Tuning events only.

items.title: Logbook entries
items.text:
Where the logbook integration is turned on (the LOGBOOK_ENABLED setting):

  • DTM makes a logbook entry when an operator creates or closes an incident, with its summary, times and cause, and a link back to DTM. Actions taken as Reviewer make no entries.
  • The incident table has a Log Entries column listing entries that reference the incident. Create New Log Entry opens a new logbook entry already referencing it (dtm:<incident ID>), and View Interval ± 1Hr opens the logbook from an hour before the incident to an hour after.

Make logbook entries for an incident from DTM, so they are tagged with it: anyone (operators, technicians, engineers, managers) can add to the incident's record that way, and the entries form its timeline.

items.title: Other tools
items.text:
• Incident page. Each incident has a page with all its details, at /dtm/incidents/<incident ID>; select the * next to its ID in the incident table to copy the link. Events have links too, at /dtm/events/<event ID>.
  • Wall display. /dtm/wall is a full-screen list of open events for a control room screen. It updates every minute.
  • Downgrade Readiness. Where the SRM integration is on, incidents on systems that SRM tracks have a Downgrade Readiness link, which opens an SRM signoff for that system and component marked Not Ready.
  • Escalation. Where it is set up, DTM posts to the control room bulletin board when an event has been open for 2 hours, and again at 4 hours.
  • Shift summaries. On Open, Current Shift Summary and Previous Shift Summary open the Incident Downtime report for the shift (Owl 23:00–07:00, Day 07:00–15:00, Swing 15:00–23:00).

items.title: Reports
items.text:
User Guide › Reports

DTM's reports are on three tabs: Reports for downtime and trip statistics, Operability for the regular availability and repair reviews, and Beam Transport for tuning. Anyone can view them without logging in, except Activity Audit, which is for administrators.

These numbers are for understanding system performance. They aren't the official DOE availability figures, which come from BTM.

items.title: Using the report pages
items.text:
• Choose... opens a report's filters; Apply runs it. Some reports also have Reset and Clear links.
  • Date Range offers presets (fiscal years and their quarters, calendar years, months, weeks starting Wednesday, crew chief shifts, the past 3, 7 or 10 days, yesterday, today) and Custom.... The presets' days start at 7:00. Custom start dates are inclusive and end dates exclusive. Most reports default to the past 7 days.
  • The address bar always holds the report's full settings, so you can bookmark it or send the link. Many reports share your last choices during your session, so a date range you pick on one carries over to the next.
  • Full Screen hides the page's menus. Export offers some of: Image (a PNG of the page), Print (a print-friendly page), Excel and CSV.
  • Charts can usually be shown as Bar, Pie, Pareto or Table, of downtime, count or mean time to recover. Select a label or bar to drill down to the next report.

items.title: How downtime is counted
items.text:
• Durations are bounded by the date range: only the part of an event or incident inside the range counts. Hover over a duration to see the full, unbounded one. Open events and incidents count up to now.
  • Event downtime is the time from an event's first incident down to the event's time up. It is made up of suspend time, when at least one incident is open, and restore time, when none is.
  • Incident downtime adds up every incident, so incidents at the same time are each counted in full.
  • Non-overlapping downtime merges overlapping incidents in the same system (or category) and event type, so that time is counted once.
  • Trip downtime counts FSD trips of 5 minutes or less, outside SAM (longer trips should be events). See Trips.
  • Program time is the scheduled program time from the crew chief time sheets in BTM: physics, studies, restore, accelerator and down time. Uptime, MTBF and availability are worked out from it, so they are shown only for the CEBAF Blocked type.
  • MTTR (mean time to recover) is downtime divided by the number of failures; MTBF (mean time between failures) is uptime divided by the number of failures; availability is uptime as a percentage of program time.
  • Beam Transport incidents are the ones in the Beam Transport category. Most reports can exclude them, or show only them.

items.title: Reports tab
items.text: Page Shows Summary The headline numbers for one event type: event, suspend, restore and incident downtime, counts, MTTR, non-overlapping downtime and trips. For CEBAF Blocked it adds program time, uptime, MTBF, failure rates, availability and the losses due to events and trips. Select the * on a row for its definition. Root Cause Counts and hours of incidents by review level and how many aren't reviewed, then the incidents for the column you choose, with their root cause, RAR and SMEs. Defaults to the previous month's CEBAF Blocked incidents. Category Down Incident downtime, count and MTTR by alpha category, with or without merging overlaps. For CEBAF Blocked alone it adds program time, uptime, MTBF, failure rate, availability and loss. Excel and CSV export. System Down The same by system, optionally for one category. Excel export. Component Down Incident downtime, count and MTTR by component, optionally for one system, with the same CEBAF Blocked columns. Incident Down Individual incidents, longest first, filtered by duration, type, system, repair group or component, with totals split into overnight (19:00–07:00) and daytime. Excel export, and a Shiftlog export of the list as a web page. Event Down Events with their downtime, restore time and incident counts. Excel export. Event Timeline The events in a period on a timeline, one row per event type. Repair Summary Repair hours or incident counts over time, by repair group. CSV export. FSD Summary FSD trip counts, rates, lost hours and average durations over time, by cause or area. Rates can be per program hour or per hour of the period. CSV export. Activity Audit Administrators only: who changed which events and incidents, when and from which computer, with each version's values. Expert The SMEs for each system, optionally for one category.

items.title: Operability
items.text:
The Operability tab has the reports used in the weekly and monthly reviews. Most of them cover the CEBAF Blocked type.

Page Shows Weekly Repair A week's top incidents (5 by default) with their solution, system and component, repairer, and how often the component failed in the last 4 weeks. Reviewers can edit an incident from here with Edit Selected. Weekly Cause The Level Ⅲ+ incidents whose RAR was uploaded during the week. Monthly Avail. The monthly availability report: overall availability against the goal and the previous month, trips and repairs, the top repairs, repairs by category, and repairs by category and day. Reviewers can edit the goals and the notes. Run Compare Accumulated downtime of several runs (date ranges you add and label), side by side. Trend Downtime, uptime and availability overall, and downtime, counts, MTTR, MTBF and availability for trips, for events and per category, in bins of a day to a year. Excel export. Annual Repair A year's CEBAF Blocked repair hours by category, stacked by month, with each month's program hours. Joule Reliability for the Joule metrics, from DTM's downtime and BTM's hours; see below. CSV export.

items.title: Joule
items.text:
The Joule report combines BTM's hours with DTM's CEBAF Blocked and CEBAF Tuning downtime:

  • Research is physics time less tuning and physics downtime, plus any Quality Hours allowance.
  • Tuning, Setup, & Restore is CEBAF Tuning downtime plus BTM's restore and accelerator time.
  • Delivered is research, studies, and tuning, setup and restore.
  • Unscheduled Failures are CEBAF Blocked downtime less the Maintenance Hours allowance.
  • Reliability is delivered time as a percentage of delivered time plus failures.
  • Budgeted hours come from the NPES schedule, times the Budget Scaler. The report also gives delivered as a percentage of budgeted, and research as a percentage of delivered time plus failures.

Allowances are spread evenly over the bins. The report can be a table or a chart: reliability per bin, reliability with its accumulated average (weighted by scheduled hours, so the last point is the whole period's reliability), delivered against budgeted progress, or delivered against failures. The reliability charts mark the DOE minimum of 80%.

items.title: Beam Transport
items.text:
The Beam Transport tab reports only Beam Transport (tuning) incidents.

Page Shows Weekly Tune A week's top tune incidents, like Weekly Repair, with the total tune time. Excel export. Tune Incidents Tune incidents in a period, newest first, filtered by type and component. Excel export. Tune Comparison Which Beam Transport components took the most tune time.

items.title: Reviewing incidents
items.text:
User Guide › Reviewing incidents

Each incident is reviewed twice:

  • the SME review, by the subject matter experts (SMEs) for the failed system, and
  • the OPR review, by Operability.

The review status shows on each event's row (an SME icon and an OPR icon: reviewed, partly reviewed or not reviewed) and in each incident's Review column (SME: Yes/No, OPR: Yes/No). Select the * next to "Review:" to see the full review.

items.title: Review levels
items.text:
An incident's review level depends on how long it lasted, and decides what the SME review needs. The incident's row shows the level as "Unknown" until the incident is closed; reports count open incidents as Level Ⅲ+ and not reviewed.

Level Incident duration The SME review is done when Level Ⅰ under 30 minutes Acknowledged is Yes Level Ⅱ 30 minutes to under 4 hours a Root Cause is given Level Ⅲ+ 4 hours or more a Repair Assessment Report (RAR) is uploaded

The expert email describes what each level involves:

  • Level Ⅰ: short repairs (5–30 minutes). Group leader or SME review: check a box. Due in 2 days.
  • Level Ⅱ: a single system, more than 30 minutes of repair. Review and a root cause statement. Due in 2 days.
  • Level Ⅲ: a 4-hour escalation, or at the Director of Operations' discretion. A root cause memo using the Level Ⅲ template, and a 3–4 minute report at the next Weekly Summary Meeting.
  • Level Ⅳ: a program change, a safety issue, a compounded event, or at the Director of Operations' discretion. A Repair Investigation Team, using the Level Ⅳ template, within 3 weeks.

DTM itself doesn't tell Level Ⅲ and Ⅳ apart: both are Level Ⅲ+. Reports count an incident with a RAR as reviewed whatever its level. The RAR Procedure has the details.

items.title: Who the SMEs are
items.text: Each system has a list of experts, kept by the DTM administrators on Setup › Expert List (and shown on Reports › Expert). When an incident is created, or its system is changed, the system's experts become the incident's SME Reviewer(s). To assign other experts, edit the incident and change Reviewer(s) (usernames separated by spaces) on the Explained tab. Whenever the SMEs change, the incident's acknowledgement goes back to No.

items.title: Expert email
items.text: Where email is turned on, each weekday at 9:55 DTM emails every SME who has closed incidents that aren't acknowledged from the last 24 hours (72 hours on Mondays). The email lists the incidents with links, a DTM-RAR Review link to the SME's unacknowledged incidents, and the action level table above. Administrators can preview it, or send it to one person, from Setup › Email.

items.title: Doing the review
items.text:
1. Find the incident: follow the link in the email, or on Events filter by SME and Expert Acknowledged.
  2. Select Edit SME Review on the incident's row (or on its incident page).
  3. Fill in what the incident's level needs:
  4. Acknowledged (Level Ⅰ): Yes, or Reassign if it was assigned to the wrong expert.
  5. Root Cause (Level Ⅱ): what caused the failure, up to 512 characters.
  6. Repair Assessment Report [RAR] (Level Ⅲ+): choose the report file (PDF, Word or text, up to 10 MB). It uploads as soon as you choose it; uploading again replaces it.
  7. Select Save.

Giving a root cause also sets Acknowledged to Yes; uploading a RAR doesn't, so set it to Yes as well, or the incident stays on your list of unacknowledged incidents. Reassign only marks the incident; nobody is notified, so change its Reviewer(s) or tell Operability who the right expert is.

items.title: OPR review
items.text:
Operability reviewers (the dtm-reviewer role, acting as Reviewer) review each incident's record: they correct it where needed, then select Edit Incident, open the Explained tab and fill in:

  • Reviewer: the reviewer's username (Me fills in yours),
  • Repairer: the groups that repaired it,
  • Solution: how it was fixed.

Incidents can be OPR reviewed while their event is still open, which helps with long degraded events.

Once an incident has an OPR reviewer, operators can no longer change it or its event; reviewers still can. Reviewers can also change events that closed more than 10 hours ago. Changes made as Reviewer don't create logbook entries; switch to Operator in the menu next to your name if you want them.

The Operability tab's weekly and monthly repair pages have reviewer-only editing too; see Reports.

items.title: RAR tab
items.text:
The RAR tab lists the incidents that have a Repair Assessment Report, with their hours, the problem and component, the root cause, the report's Download link and upload date, and the SMEs with whether the incident is reviewed. It opens on the previous month's CEBAF Blocked incidents; change that with Choose..., and sort by duration, time down or upload date.

Its buttons open the Procedure and the Level Ⅲ Template and Level Ⅳ Template documents.

items.title: RARs for SAM periods
items.text:
Add SAM RAR records a RAR that doesn't belong to a downtime incident, such as one for work during a scheduled accelerator maintenance (SAM) period. It creates a closed CEBAF Blocked event with one Unknown/Missing incident to hold the report. That event is counted like any other, so its hours appear in the CEBAF Blocked downtime reports.

To add one:

  1. Select Add SAM RAR, enter a Title and Time Down. Time Up defaults to 4 hours after the time down.
  2. Select Next, choose the report file, then select Done.

These events must not overlap other CEBAF Blocked events. If the exact time doesn't matter, use a 4-hour block starting at midnight on the first day of the SAM, and put further SAM RARs on different days. Operators can only add them for the last 10 hours; a reviewer can add older ones.

items.title: Finding incidents that need review
items.text:
• Reports › Root Cause lists incidents with their review level, root cause and SMEs, filtered by All Incidents, Not Reviewed or a single level.
  • Events, filtered by SME and Expert Acknowledged, shows one expert's incidents.

items.title: Trips
items.text:
User Guide › Trips

The Trips tab lists Fast ShutDown (FSD) trips: short interruptions when the FSD system removes beam because of a fault. DTM gets them from the FSD system; nobody enters or edits them in DTM.

A trip that lasts more than 5 minutes should be recorded as a downtime event, with an incident for the component that caused it (see Recording downtime). DTM doesn't do this for you. That is also why reports count only trips of 5 minutes or less as trip downtime: longer ones are counted through their incidents.

items.title: The list
items.text:
Each row shows the faulted systems (joined with "+", or "<< PHANTOM >>" when no system is known, with "(N)" when more than one device faulted and "^" while the trip is still open), when it went down and how long it lasted. Hover over the time for seconds, and over the duration for the time up.

Click a row to expand it:

  • Cause and Area, which DTM works out from the faulted devices. Causes include a device category such as Magnets or Vacuum, "Hall", "Multiple/Other", "Unknown/Missing", and finer ones such as "RF (C25/50)", "RF (Multi/Other)", "MPS (BLM)" or "Dump (Insert.)". Areas are Accelerator, Accelerator (RF), Hall A to D, Multiple or Unknown.
  • Trip ID.
  • Machine State: the accelerator's and each hall's state when it tripped.
  • Faulted FSD Channel: the node, channel and path, with each faulted device's category, system, CED type and name, whether it is confirmed, and its region.

items.title: Filtering
items.text:
Open the filter with Choose...:

  • Date Range: trips that started in the range.
  • Min Trip Duration, Max Trip Duration, in seconds, minutes or hours.
  • Machine State: the accelerator state (PHYSICS, OFF, DOWN, ACC, RESTORE, STUDIES) and each hall's state (OFF, DOWN, TUNE, BANU, UP).
  • Cause, Area, System, CED Type, CED Name: text, with % as a wildcard.
  • Max CED Types Per Trip, Max Devices Per Trip, the FSD Node and Channel #, and Trip ID.

Show 10, 25 or 100 trips per page. Export downloads the list as CSV (one row per trip) or CSV (Exploded) (one row per faulted device). The export doesn't apply the Area and Machine State filters, so it can have more rows than the page.

The trip reports are Reports › FSD Summary and the trip counts in Reports › Downtime Summary; see Reports.
